result.question: How do wineries, distilleries, and alcohol-discovery platforms (Vivino, Untappd, Distiller, Whisky Exchange, Master of Malt, winery direct-to-consumer sites) present, structure, and sell the full spectrum of alcohol — wine (including tastings, terroir, how each wine is made, wine history), whiskey, gin, vodka, rum — and what open or permissible data sources exist (open datasets, APIs, Wikidata, public domain databases) for ingesting spirits/wine/cocktail data with clean provenance into a consumer night-out-planning app? Focus: (1) data models they use per category (tasting notes, ratings scales, production/distillery metadata), (2) how they merchandise/sell (editorial storytelling vs data), (3) ratings/review UX patterns that drive engagement, (4) concretely ingestable permissible sources with licence notes. The app is PUBMAXXING (London pub map, real pint prices, provenance-honest community layer) expanding from beer to all alcohol.
result.summary: The leading alcohol-discovery platforms converge on crowd-first rating models deliberately simpler than expert scales: Vivino uses a 1-5 star system (0.5 granularity) chosen for Amazon/TripAdvisor familiarity and legitimized by a claimed 4.0-star ≈ 90-point expert correlation across 100k+ expert ratings, while Untappd layers per-entity aggregation rules (pure average per drink, weighted per brand, Bayesian average with 150-rating minimums and 15-day recency windows for local top-rated lists) plus anti-noise thresholds (ratings hidden under 10 votes, check-ins distinct from ratings). Engagement is driven by durable gamification keyed to structured product metadata — ABV-threshold badges, streaks, and location challenges persisted essentially unchanged 2020-2025 — and these crowd scores have real commercial gravity (Tavour and EeBria gate purchasing/partnership on Untappd thresholds). Crucially, neither Vivino nor Untappd is a permissible data source: Vivino has no public API and researchers had to scrape it, so PUBMAXXING's clean-provenance ingestion should come from Wikidata (CC0, no attribution required, policy-excluded non-open data), Open Food Facts (ODbL/DbCL/CC-BY-SA with rate limits and bulk dumps), the US TTB Public COLA Registry (public-domain government label metadata with 1999+ label images, ~48h latency), and TheCocktailDB (free test key for prototyping, $10 one-off for full cocktail taxonomy of name/ingredient/category/glass/alcoholic-status). The strategic pattern for PUBMAXXING: replicate the platforms' UX mechanics (simple stars, Bayesian/recency-weighted local lists, metadata-keyed badges) while sourcing the underlying product graph exclusively from open/permissive datasets the incumbents themselves do not offer.

findings.claim: Vivino's rating model is a deliberately consumer-familiar 1-5 star scale (0.5 granularity), chosen over the 100-point expert scale because stars are familiar from Amazon/TripAdvisor; Vivino legitimizes crowd scores by claiming (from 100,000+ expert ratings analyzed) that a 4.0 community rating correlates with a 90-point expert (Parker/Wine Enthusiast) score, and by sheer volume (1.4M wines rated by users 2011-2015 vs 370k by the seven most prolific experts).
findings.vote: unanimous across 4 merged claims (3-0 each), one at 2-1 elsewhere; these four all 3-0
findings.evidence: Vivino's own page: 'This kind of rating system is familiar to consumers... popularized by companies like Amazon, TripAdvisor'; 'We looked at more than 100,000 expert ratings... a 4.0 Vivino rating correlates with a 90 point expert rating.' Peer-reviewed ASONAM 2018 paper independently reports the same correlation claim and the 1.4M-vs-370k volume figures. Caveat: the correlation figure is Vivino marketing with unpublished methodology; an independent 2025 Journal of Wine Economics study found substantial but weaker crowd-critic correlation (~40% vs 63% critic-critic).

findings.claim: Vivino publishes rating-distribution anchors as merchandising signals: across its (then) 9.5M-wine database the average rating is 3.6, a 4.0 beats 85% of wines, and a 4.5 beats 99% — percentile framing that converts a star score into a purchase heuristic.
findings.evidence: Vivino: 'the average Vivino rating is a 3.6... Wines that are rated 4.0... are ranked better than 85 percent of the 9.5 million wines... Wines rated 4.5... are better than 99 percent.' The 9.5M figure is a dated snapshot (Vivino now cites ~17M wines) but the distribution anchors remain Vivino's published guidance. Directly reusable UX pattern for PUBMAXXING: show where a pub/drink sits in the distribution, not just the raw average.

findings.claim: Untappd uses different rating aggregation per entity level and explicit anti-noise/anti-gaming rules: pure unweighted average on drink pages, weighted average on brand pages, Bayesian averages for Top Rated lists (150-rating minimum per drink; Local variant counts only check-ins from the last 15 days within the search radius), ratings suppressed until a drink has 10+ ratings, and check-ins (activity) are distinct from ratings (blank ratings never count as zero).
findings.evidence: Untappd's official help doc (verified live/archived June 2026): 'The Drink Pure Average... is calculated as the pure average'; 'The Brand Average... is calculated as a weighted average across the brand's drinks'; 'A drink must have 150 ratings to qualify for the Top Rated list... calculated by a Bayesian Average of drinks checked in within the last 15 days in the selected search radius'; 'A drink needs at least 10 ratings before the rating will show'; blank ratings 'do not count toward the drink's total.' This is a complete, copyable rating-integrity architecture for a pub/pint-rating app.

findings.claim: Untappd's engagement engine is gamification keyed directly to structured product metadata: badges triggered by ABV thresholds (e.g. 'Sky's the Limit' for 10%+ ABV beers, 'Middle of the Road' for 5-10%), plus streak/frequency badges ('Drinking Your Paycheck' — five drinks on a Friday; 'Daily Checker' — seven consecutive daily check-ins) and location-based challenges. These core mechanics persisted essentially unchanged from 2020 to 2025, suggesting they are the durable engagement drivers — though academic work flags documented ethical concerns about gamifying repeated alcohol consumption.
findings.evidence: Longitudinal 2020-vs-2025 academic study: 'the platform's core gaming mechanics (i.e. badges, streaks, and location-based challenges) remain unchanged'; ABV and streak badges quoted verbatim and corroborated by Untappd community badge guides and Untappd's own product-update channels (only incremental badge/UI changes 2022-2024). Design implication for PUBMAXXING: structured drink metadata (ABV, style, venue) can directly power engagement loops, but streak mechanics that reward consumption frequency carry ethical/duty-of-care risk for an alcohol app — the 'durable drivers' inference is reasonable but goes slightly beyond what the paper measured.

findings.claim: Crowd ratings on Untappd directly gate commerce: US e-retailer Tavour requires five or more beers rated above 4 stars with 100+ ratings each before partnering with a brewery, and UK marketplace EeBria observes purchase rates only ramp up above a 3.7 average (and only displays scores above 3.7) — evidence that community rating layers become de facto merchandising infrastructure.
findings.evidence: Good Beer Hunting (reputable trade journalism, 2021): Tavour email shown to reporter — 'five or more beers boasting above a four-star rating, with over 100 ratings per beer'; EeBria CEO on purchase data — 'Below 3.7 there's almost no difference at all... above that 3.7, it starts to ramp up quite nicely.' Medium confidence: single secondary source; the Tavour requirement documented via one email to one brewery; data is from 2021.

findings.claim: Vivino and Untappd data are NOT permissibly ingestable: Vivino offers no public API (researchers built a custom throttled Selenium crawler over five months; only unofficial scrapers exist today), so incumbents' catalogs cannot be sourced with clean provenance for a consumer app.
findings.evidence: ASONAM 2018 paper: 'Vivino does not offer an API to collect data from their site, therefore, we... [used] a custom web crawler... throttled... to 0.2 requests per second... over five months.' Verifier confirmed (July 2026) no official Vivino API exists — only unofficial wrappers and paid scraping services hitting internal endpoints, none of which provide licensed data. Note: the parallel claim that Vivino's per-wine schema (type/vintage/region/grapes/food-pairings) is a reusable template was REFUTED in verification, so treat Vivino's exact field list as unverified.

findings.claim: Wikidata is the cleanest-provenance open source for spirits/wine/cocktail entity data (distilleries, wineries, brands, production metadata): all structured data in the main, property, and lexeme namespaces is CC0 (public-domain-equivalent), imposing no attribution requirement and permitting commercial reuse; Wikidata policy deliberately excludes data lacking a CC0-compatible license.
findings.vote: 3-0 on two claims, 2-1 on the core CC0 claim
findings.evidence: Primary policy page (fetched 2026-07-07): 'All structured data in the main, property and lexeme namespaces is made available under the Creative Commons CC0 License'; 'Wikidata avoids hosting data that lacks a CC0 license.' CC0 waives attribution and EU sui generis database rights. Caveats: no legal guarantee every contributor lawfully released their data (per-statement provenance risk is nonzero — OSM has publicly expressed distrust of some Wikidata CC0 assertions); CC0 does not waive trademarks on brand names; Wikipedia article text and Commons images are NOT CC0 (CC BY-SA, attribution required).

findings.claim: Open Food Facts is a permissible ingestion source with clear obligations: database under ODbL, contents under the Database Contents License, images under CC-BY-SA — requiring attribution and share-alike. The read API is rate-limited (~15 req/min/IP for product queries, 10 req/min/IP for search) and the project directs bulk consumers to CSV/JSONL dumps instead.
findings.evidence: Official docs (fetched live 2026-07): licence trio stated verbatim; '15 req/min/IP address for all read product queries', '10 req/min/IP... for all search queries', 'If you need to fetch more than a few hundred products... download the data as a CSV or JSONL file directly.' Ingestion plan for PUBMAXXING: use bulk dumps, not the API; attribute OFF with a link; share-alike applies to derivative databases. Image caveat: CC-BY-SA covers only OFF's own rights — pack designs/trademarks may carry third-party rights needing case-by-case review.

findings.claim: The US TTB Public COLA Registry is a free, no-registration, public-domain government database of alcohol label approvals (wine, spirits, malt beverages) covering approved/expired/surrendered/revoked COLAs, with actual label images viewable for COLAs from 1999 to present and new approvals appearing roughly 48 hours after approval — a concretely ingestable source of near-current US product label metadata.
findings.evidence: TTB primary source (verified live 2026-07-07): 'No registration or password is required'; images 'available for viewing and printing for COLAs issued from 1999 to present and are generally available 48 hours after they have been approved'; also listed on data.gov as a downloadable Treasury dataset. Caveats: US-only coverage (limited direct use for a London app beyond imported brands); no formal bulk API (search-and-download); label artwork itself may carry brand copyright/trademark, so redisplaying images is a separate licensing question from ingesting the metadata.

findings.claim: TheCocktailDB is a zero-cost cocktail data source for prototyping (test API key '1' explicitly permitted for development/educational use; basic API 'free forever'), with full-database access behind a one-off $10 Premium upgrade (free tier: 100-item list cap, no multi-ingredient filter, no Popular/Recent endpoints). Its data model — search by name/letter/ID, filter by ingredient, alcoholic status, category, and glass type, plus random-cocktail and ingredient-lookup endpoints — is a taxonomy directly mappable to PUBMAXXING's drinks schema.
findings.evidence: Primary vendor page fetched and endpoints live-tested 2026-07-07: strCategory/strAlcoholic/strGlass fields confirmed in real responses. Critical provenance caveat (a companion claim was REFUTED on this exact point in the opposite direction, so treat carefully): the site grants API access tiers but no explicit open-data licence for bulk ingestion/redistribution — fine for prototyping via API, but permanent data ingest with clean provenance needs direct clarification from the maintainers. Production/app-store release requires the paid Premium key.

result.caveats: Key uncertainties: (1) Vivino's expert-correlation figure (4.0 ≈ 90 points) is first-party marketing with no published methodology — an independent 2025 Journal of Wine Economics study found weaker crowd-critic agreement, so present it as Vivino's claim, not fact. (2) The Vivino per-product schema claim (fields like vintage/grapes/food-pairings) was refuted in verification, so no verified template exists for Vivino's data model — only its rating system. (3) TheCocktailDB's licence status for permanent bulk ingestion is genuinely ambiguous: the claim that its page states no open-data licence was itself voted down 0-3, yet the surviving claims also note no explicit redistribution grant; resolve directly with the maintainers before ingesting rather than merely calling the API. (4) Time-sensitivity: Vivino's 9.5M-wine figure and the 2011-2015 volume comparison are dated (Vivino now cites ~17M wines); Tavour/EeBria commercial-gating evidence is from 2021 and single-sourced. (5) The Untappd 'durable engagement drivers' finding infers engagement value from feature persistence — the underlying paper measured persistence and ethical concerns, not engagement causality. (6) TTB is US-only and OFF image/TTB label imagery may embed third-party brand rights regardless of the database licence. (7) One core Wikidata CC0 claim passed only 2-1; per-statement provenance in Wikidata is community-enforced, not legally guaranteed.
openQuestions: What do wine/spirits platforms' actual per-product data models look like in verified detail (tasting-note structure, production metadata, terroir fields)? The Vivino schema claim was refuted and no Distiller, Whisky Exchange, or Master of Malt claims survived verification, leaving the 'editorial storytelling vs data' merchandising axis and whisky/gin-specific modelling essentially unanswered.

Is there a UK/EU equivalent of the TTB COLA Registry (e.g. HMRC, Food Standards Agency, or EU e-Ambrosia/PDO-PGI registers) providing open label or product-approval data relevant to a London-focused app?
Will TheCocktailDB's maintainers grant an explicit licence for bulk ingestion and redistribution of cocktail data (beyond API prototyping), and what are the terms?

What is the actual coverage and quality of alcohol entities in Wikidata and Open Food Facts for London-relevant products (UK gins, cask ales, wines sold in UK pubs) — i.e., is the permissible data sufficient in practice, not just in licence?

refuted.claim: Vivino's wine data model per product comprises: name, type (white/red/rosé/port/dessert/sparkling), vintage, average price, average rating, number of ratings, ratings breakdown, country, region, regional style, winery, food pairings, and grapes — a directly reusable schema template for an all-alcohol product model.

The API terms page states no explicit open-data licence, attribution requirement, or commercial-use grant, so provenance/licence status for ingesting its data into a commercial app is undefined on the official page and would need direct clarification.

Untappd's rating UX is built on a 1–5 star scale combined with location-tagged check-ins and gamified badges awarded for actions like checking in beers within style categories — a model that drives engagement of roughly 90,000–100,000 new U.S. registered users per month.
